note: Verification methods for an AI agent's natural-language report of what it did, plotted by added latency per response (log ms) versus the share of fabricated claims they catch (detection coverage). Detection/FPR/latency for the five output-checking methods are from Table 3 of Basu, 'Tool Receipts, Not Zero-Knowledge Proofs' (arXiv:2603.10060). The cryptographic extreme (zkLLM) and the chain-native receipt are reference anchors: zkLLM proves the forward pass, not tool truth, at minutes per query (Chen et al., zkLLM, CCS 2024); the chain receipt is the consensus-settled log of an on-chain action, read in roughly one RPC round-trip and deterministic. The 100ms wall marks the rough threshold above which added latency stops feeling instant to an interactive agent's user.

claimTypes.label: On-chain action
claimTypes.example: "I swapped 134 WETH and 13,186 USDC into a liquidity position."
claimTypes.why: The chain already wrote an unforgeable receipt: status, gas, and the exact Transfer/Mint logs. Reading it is deterministic and consensus-backed — no proof to generate, nothing for the model to fake.

claimTypes.label: Off-chain tool output
claimTypes.example: "The price API returned 5 venues; the best quote was $1,731.40."
claimTypes.why: No blockchain witnesses an HTTPS call, but the agent's own runtime can: sign every tool execution and check the model's claimed counts/facts against the receipt. ~12 ms, no model in the loop.

claimTypes.label: Inference correctness
claimTypes.example: "This summary was produced by the model you paid for, unaltered."
claimTypes.why: Proving the forward pass itself was the named model needs cryptography — zkLLM or re-execution. It is the one claim a receipt cannot make, and it costs minutes per query.

claimTypes.label: Free reasoning / opinion
claimTypes.example: "I considered the gas environment and decided now was the cheapest moment."
claimTypes.why: No receipt exists, because nothing was executed. The honest engineering move is to label it as ungrounded — not to assert it as a verified fact. Every verifier here abstains.

methods.label: Chain receipt
methods.verifies: On-chain actions — transfers, swaps, contract calls — from the block's own logs.
methods.note: An EIP-2718 receipt commits to status, gas used, and a logs array, sealed into the block by consensus. Verifying "the swap happened, for exactly these amounts" is a log lookup, not a proof. It is the cheapest verifier that exists — but it only witnesses what touched the chain.

methods.label: Output regex
methods.verifies: Surface patterns in the text — malformed counts, obvious format breaks.
methods.note: Almost free and never wrong about syntax, but blind to a confident, well-formed lie. Catches roughly a third of fabrications.

methods.label: Signed tool receipts
methods.verifies: Each claim against an HMAC-signed record of the tool call that supposedly produced it.
methods.note: NabaOS: the runtime hashes every tool input/output into a signed receipt the model can't forge, then cross-checks claimed counts and facts. 94.2% of fabricated tool calls, 87.6% of count mismatches, 91.3% of false-absence claims — at under 15 ms, no second model in the loop.

methods.label: SVIP-style probe
methods.verifies: Internal-signal heuristics on the generation itself.
methods.note: Cheaper than a full re-generation and better than regex, but still a guess about whether the model is grounded — a 10% false-positive rate flags honest answers too.

methods.label: RAG re-grounding
methods.note: Pays a retrieval round-trip per response and still misses half the fabrications, while flagging nearly one honest claim in five. Adds latency the user feels.

methods.label: Self-consistency
methods.verifies: Whether the model agrees with itself across samples.
methods.note: Re-runs the generation several times and compares. Multiplies cost and seconds of latency to catch fewer than half of fabrications — a correlated model fails the same way every time.

methods.label: zkLLM proof
methods.verifies: That the forward pass was the named model, bit-exact — not whether a tool output is real.
methods.note: A genuine cryptographic guarantee, and the right tool when the inference itself is the disputed object. But it is thousands of times slower than plain inference — minutes per query — and it still says nothing about whether the API the agent quoted actually returned what it claims.
